newsitem.title: USA: Assets Surge For U.S. Institutions.
newsitem.headline: Assets Surge For U.S. Institutions.

text.p: U.S. institutional investors held more than $11.1 trillion in total assets at the end of the second quarter of 1996, up from $10.5 trillion at the end of 1995 and $6.3 trillion in 1990, according to a report from the Conference Board.

Investment companies, including mutual funds, showed the greatest growth in assets, while pension funds showed the biggest declines, according to the Institutional Investment Report, which tracks total assets of U.S. institutional investors and equity control of U.S. securities markets.

"These data are important because they indicate changes in the balance of power between corporate managements and institutional shareholders," says Carolyn Kay Brancato, the report's principal author.

At the end of the second quarter of 1996, pension funds held 46.8 percent of assets at the end of the second quarter of 1996, investment companies (including mutual funds) had 20.2 percent, insurance companies had 19 percent, banks had 11.9 percent, and foundations had two percent.
In 1990, pension funds had 49.4 percent, insurance companies had 21 percent, investment companies had 15.3 percent, banks had 12 percent, and foundations had 2.3 percent.
According to the report, U.S. institutions controlled 47.4 percent of the U.S. equity market at the second quarter of 1996, up from roughly a third in 1980.
The institutions have tended to invest more heavily in the largest companies, and have increased holdings to slightly more than 57 percent of the stock of the largest 1,000 U.S. corporations.

"Among the reasons why we haven't seen institutions as a whole continue to increase their share of total U.S. equity markets is that individuals are increasing their purchases of stock directly from companies and via electronic on-line services," says Brancato.
Within the pension fund sector, public pension funds (state and local funds) are generally outpacing private trusteed funds both in total asset growth and in their allocation to equities.
During the first half of 1996, private trusteed pension funds grew only 4.3 percent compared with 8.1 percent for state and local funds.
Also, public pension funds continued their aggressive equity investment program, devoting a record 52.6 percent of total assets to equities.

The development "represents a substantial recent move into equities, as these public pension funds become more aggressive investors and depend less on bonds for portfolio investments," the report concluded.
